title: No. 53 — The Same Subject Continued (The House of Representatives) (Madison)
paragraphs: I will be reminded here, perhaps, of the common saying, "where annual elections end, tyranny begins." If it is true, as has often been remarked, that proverbial sayings are generally founded in reason, it is no less true that, once established, they are often applied to cases their reason does not cover. I need not look beyond the case before us for proof. What is the reason on which this proverbial saying rests? No one will subject himself to ridicule by pretending that any natural connection exists between the sun or the seasons and the period within which human virtue can withstand the temptations of power. Happily for humankind, liberty is not, in this respect, confined to any single point in time. It lies between extremes that allow enough latitude for all the variations required by the various situations and circumstances of civil society. The election of magistrates might be daily, weekly, or monthly, as well as annual, if it were thought useful, as in some instances it actually has been. And if circumstances may require deviating from the rule on one side, why not on the other side too? Looking at the periods established among ourselves for electing the most numerous branches of the State legislatures, we find them by no means coinciding any more than they do for elections of other civil magistrates. In Connecticut and Rhode Island, the periods are every six months. In the other States, except South Carolina, they are annual. In South Carolina they are biennial — as proposed for the federal government. Here is a difference of four to one between the longest and shortest periods. Yet it would not be easy to show that Connecticut or Rhode Island is better governed, or enjoys a greater share of rational liberty, than South Carolina. Nor is either of these States distinguished in these respects, for these reasons, from the States whose elections differ from both.

In searching for the grounds of this doctrine, I can find only one, and it does not apply to our case. The important distinction so well understood in America — between a Constitution established by the people and unalterable by the government, and a law established by the government and alterable by the government — seems to have been little understood and even less observed in any other country. Wherever the supreme legislative power has resided, it has been supposed that full power to change the form of government also resides there. Even in Great Britain, where the principles of political and civil liberty have been most discussed, and where we hear most of the rights of the Constitution, the authority of Parliament is held to be supreme and uncontrollable, with regard to the Constitution as well as to ordinary objects of legislation. They have accordingly, in several cases, actually changed by legislative acts some of the most fundamental articles of government. They have, in particular, changed the period of election on several occasions. On the last such occasion, they not only introduced seven-year elections in place of three-year ones, but by the same act continued themselves in office four years beyond the term for which the people had elected them. Attention to these dangerous practices has produced very natural alarm among the devotees of free government, of which frequent elections is the cornerstone. It has led them to seek some security for liberty against the danger to which it is exposed. Where no Constitution paramount to the government either existed or could be obtained, no constitutional security similar to that established in the United States could be attempted. Some other security therefore had to be sought. What better security could the case admit than selecting some simple and familiar period of time as a standard for measuring the danger of innovations, fixing the national sentiment, and uniting patriotic exertions? The most simple and familiar period of time applicable to the subject was a year. Hence the doctrine has been instilled by laudable zeal, to erect some barrier against the gradual innovations of an unlimited government, that the advance toward tyranny was to be measured by the distance of departure from the fixed point of annual elections. But what need is there to apply this expedient to a government limited, as the federal government will be, by the authority of a paramount Constitution? Or who will pretend that the liberties of the people of America will not be more secure under biennial elections, fixed unalterably by such a Constitution, than those of any other nation would be where elections were annual, or even more frequent, but subject to alteration by the ordinary power of government?
The second question is whether biennial elections are necessary or useful. The answer to this question, in the affirmative, will appear from several very obvious considerations.

No one can be a competent legislator who does not add, to upright intentions and sound judgment, a certain knowledge of the subjects on which he is to legislate. Part of this knowledge can be acquired through information available to men in private as well as public stations. Another part can only be obtained, or at least thoroughly obtained, by actual experience in the position that requires its use. The period of service should therefore, in all such cases, bear some proportion to the extent of practical knowledge needed for proper performance of the service. The period of legislative service established in most of the States for the more numerous branch is, as we have seen, one year. The question can then be put in this simple form: does the period of two years bear no greater proportion to the knowledge needed for federal legislation than one year does to the knowledge needed for State legislation? Merely stating the question this way suggests the answer that ought to be given.

In a single State, the necessary knowledge concerns the existing laws, which are uniform throughout the State and with which all the citizens are more or less familiar. It also concerns the general affairs of the State, which lie within a small compass, are not very diverse, and occupy much of the attention and conversation of every class of people. The great theater of the United States presents a very different scene. The laws are far from uniform — they vary in every State. Meanwhile, the public affairs of the Union are spread over a very extensive region. They are extremely diversified by the local affairs connected with them, and can hardly be correctly learned anywhere except in the central councils to which the representatives of every part of the empire bring knowledge of them. Yet some knowledge of the affairs, and even the laws, of all the States ought to be possessed by the members from each State. How can foreign trade be properly regulated by uniform laws without some acquaintance with the commerce, the ports, the customs, and the regulations of the different States? How can trade between the different States be properly regulated without some knowledge of their relative situations in these and other respects? How can taxes be judiciously imposed and effectively collected if they are not adapted to the different laws and local circumstances relating to these objects in the different States? How can uniform regulations for the militia be properly provided without similar knowledge of the many internal circumstances by which the States differ from each other? These are the principal objects of federal legislation. They strongly suggest the extensive information that representatives ought to acquire. The other domestic objects will require a proportional degree of information regarding them.

It is true that all these difficulties will, by degrees, be greatly diminished. The most laborious task will be the proper inauguration of the government and the initial formation of a federal code. Improvements on the first drafts will every year become both easier and fewer. Past transactions of the government will be a ready and accurate source of information for new members. The affairs of the Union will become more and more objects of curiosity and conversation among citizens at large. And the increased exchange among those of different States will contribute much to spreading mutual knowledge of their affairs. This in turn will contribute to a general assimilation of their manners and laws. But with all these reductions, the business of federal legislation must continue to so far exceed, in both novelty and difficulty, the legislative business of a single State, that the longer period of service assigned to those who transact it is justified.

There is a branch of knowledge belonging to a federal representative that has not yet been mentioned: foreign affairs. In regulating our own commerce, he ought to be acquainted not only with the treaties between the United States and other nations, but also with the commercial policy and laws of other nations. He ought not to be wholly ignorant of the law of nations. As far as it is a proper object of municipal legislation, that subject is committed to the federal government. Although the House of Representatives does not directly participate in foreign negotiations and arrangements, the necessary connection between the several branches of public affairs means these particular branches will frequently deserve attention in the ordinary course of legislation. Sometimes they will demand particular legislative sanction and cooperation. Some portion of this knowledge can no doubt be acquired in a man's study. But some of it can only be derived from the public sources of information. And all of it will be acquired most effectively by practical attention to the subject during actual service in the legislature.

There are other considerations, perhaps less important, but not unworthy of notice. The distance many representatives will be obliged to travel, and the arrangements that distance makes necessary, would be a much more serious objection for fit men if service were limited to a single year, than if it were extended to two years. No argument can be drawn on this subject from the case of the delegates to the existing Congress. They are elected annually, true, but their re-election is considered by the legislative assemblies almost a matter of course. The election of representatives by the people would not be governed by the same principle.

A few of the members, as happens in all such assemblies, will possess superior talents. By frequent reelections they will become long-standing members. They will thoroughly master the public business and perhaps not be unwilling to take advantage of those advantages. The greater the proportion of new members, and the less the information of the bulk of the members, the more apt they will be to fall into the snares laid for them. This remark is no less applicable to the relationship between the House of Representatives and the Senate.

Even in single States that are large and hold only one legislative session a year, frequent elections carry an inconvenience along with their advantages. False elections cannot be investigated and annulled in time for the decision to have its proper effect. If a return can be obtained, no matter by what unlawful means, the irregular member, who takes his seat as a matter of course, is sure to hold it long enough to serve his purposes. This gives a very harmful encouragement to the use of unlawful means for obtaining irregular returns. If federal legislative elections were annual, this practice could become a very serious abuse, particularly in the more distant States. Each house is, as it must be, the judge of the elections, qualifications, and returns of its members. Whatever improvements experience may suggest for simplifying and speeding the process in disputed cases, so much of a year would unavoidably elapse before an illegitimate member could be removed from his seat that the prospect of such an event would be little check on unfair and illicit means of obtaining a seat.
All these considerations taken together justify us in affirming this. Biennial elections will be as useful to the affairs of the public as we have seen they will be safe to the liberty of the people.
